claims.text: A thin, conformal Ni coating can be applied to the tungsten phase before consolidation by electroless plating or sputter deposition.
The coating will form a continuous interfacial layer between W and Cu.
Unmodified W–Cu composites develop phase separation and voids at W/Cu interfaces under elevated temperature and irradiation.
The Ni coating acts as a diffusion barrier at the W/Cu interface.
A uniform nanoscale Ni interlayer enhances bonding between the two adjoining phases.
The Ni interlayer reduces interfacial defects.
The Ni interlayer reduces W–Cu interdiffusion.
The Ni interlayer reduces the effect of thermal-expansion mismatch between W and Cu.
Enhanced metallurgical bonding stabilizes the W/Cu interface against void formation and phase segregation during thermal cycling and irradiation.
The stabilized interface promotes continuous heat-transfer pathways.
Ni-coated W–Cu composites will have fewer interfacial voids than uncoated W–Cu composites after thermal and irradiation exposure.
Ni-coated W–Cu composites will exhibit less phase separation than uncoated composites after exposure.
Ni-coated W–Cu composites will retain higher effective thermal conductivity than untreated composites under operational heat-transfer and irradiation conditions.
Untreated W–Cu interfacial voids and phase separation cause lower thermal performance.
The Ni intervention is expected to remain effective at temperatures up to approximately 350 °C.
The Ni intervention is expected to remain effective at irradiation doses representative of plasma-facing joints.
Coating thickness and uniformity may affect the outcome.
The long-term stability of the Ni interlayer under cyclic thermal and irradiation stress is unresolved.
Secondary phases may form at Ni/Cu or Ni/W boundaries.
Magnetron-sputtered Ti/Ni coatings have improved interfacial bonding in SPS-consolidated HEA/diamond composites relative to uncoated composites.
